shows.title: Sculptures
shows.description:
Baldessari spent so much of his career associated with photo-text works and painted-over film stills that his sculptural output tends to get treated as a footnote. This show argues otherwise, gathering pieces that show him thinking just as rigorously in three dimensions, whether through patterned wallpaper, bas-relief, or freestanding objects that play with scale the way his 2D work played with cropping and juxtaposition.

The anchor piece on view, "Beethoven's Trumpet (With Ear) Opus #133," is vintage late Baldessari absurdism: an oversized bronze horn fused to a giant ceramic ear mounted on the wall, a sly, slightly grotesque sight gag about listening, music, and the body that also functions as a working speaker. It's the kind of one-liner-with-depth that made Baldessari's photo-text pieces so durable, translated here into a physically imposing object you have to walk around.

For a gallery best known for museum-scale photography and painting exhibitions, this is a chance to see one of Los Angeles's defining conceptual artists from an angle even longtime followers may not have considered.

shows.title: Broken Sleeps
shows.description:
Fiona Connor has built her practice around a kind of forensic replication: painstakingly recreating overlooked public fixtures, noticeboards, screen doors, drinking fountains, so precisely that the copy becomes a way of making a familiar, ignored object suddenly visible again. This new body of work continues that project, using cast and fabricated versions of everyday infrastructure to sit somewhere between sculpture, readymade, and quiet civic portraiture.

The New Zealand-born, Los Angeles-based artist has had this material treated seriously by institutions (MOCA, the Modern Art Oxford) precisely because of what it withholds: there's no dramatic gesture here, just an insistence that the overlooked apparatus of shared public space deserves the same attention as any other sculptural subject.

Château Shatto has built its reputation on exactly this kind of rigorous, research-driven conceptual program, and Connor's show is a good example of why the gallery is considered one of the more serious spaces for younger and mid-career artists working in this vein in Los Angeles.

shows.title: Book of Sand
shows.description:
Elliott Hundley's seventh solo show with Regen Projects, "Book of Sand," turns the gallery into something like a therapist's sand tray blown up to room scale. Hundley has long built his paintings and sculptures out of accumulation — pins, paper cut-outs, string, encaustic, found objects layered obsessively onto panel and linen — and here he pushes that method toward automatism, working without a predetermined narrative and letting the compulsive act of collecting and arranging become the subject itself.

The show borrows its title from Borges' short story about an infinite, unreadable book, and its conceptual backbone from Jungian sandplay therapy, in which patients arrange miniature figures in sand to surface unconscious material that resists language. Certain paintings in the show are literally bordered like a sand tray, turning the gallery walls into a kind of psychic arena. The centerpiece sculpture, "Palette" (2024), is a towering totem of concrete, steel, rope, bone, feathers and a dozen other materials Hundley has been hoarding in his studio; a large tapestry incorporates fragments of the veil his mother wore at her wedding, folding personal history directly into the work's fabric.

Hundley — a UCLA MFA and longtime L.A. fixture whose work sits in the collections of the Whitney, MoMA, LACMA and the Hammer — has always used maximalist accumulation to talk about grief, memory and desire without resorting to straightforward narrative. This show, freed from the Greek tragedies and modernist poetry that anchored his earlier bodies of work, feels like the most interior and least literary version of that project yet. It runs concurrently with a focused viewing-room presentation of small watercolor paintings by the late Silke Otto-Knapp, making a visit to Regen Projects worth two shows in one trip.

shows.title: Hard Line Women
shows.description:
"Hard Line Women" traces a lineage of Japanese women artists who pushed against the edges of painting, sculpture, and performance from the postwar decades up through today. The gallery — which has spent years building a reputation for introducing major, under-recognized Japanese artists to American audiences — pulls together figures like Sumie Aoki and Saori (Madokoro) Akutagawa, whose gestural, boldly graphic paintings from the 1950s and 60s read as forceful rather than decorative, alongside later and contemporary artists working across painting, installation, and photography.

The show's title gets at its central argument: that these artists, often sidelined in favor of their male peers within Japan's postwar avant-garde movements, worked with a directness and structural rigor that has been underappreciated. Akutagawa's paintings in particular, with their flattened, high-contrast figures and confident line, feel newly relevant alongside younger artists still negotiating similar questions of gesture and abstraction.

This is exactly the kind of exhibition Nonaka-Hill does best: a historically minded group show that treats its subjects as serious contributors to art history rather than a footnote, presented in a gallery that has become one of the more thoughtful spaces in the city for encountering Japanese art outside the usual blue-chip names.

shows.title: Form Follows Feeling
shows.description:
Oliver Lee Jackson has spent over five decades making paintings that refuse to sit still — figures dissolve into color fields, abstract marks harden into bodies, and compositions built from bronze paint, applied cloth, and glitter shift register from panel to panel. "Form Follows Feeling" brings together recent and older paintings that show just how consistent his restless, intuitive method has remained since the 1970s, when he first developed the dense, layered surfaces that still define his work.

Jackson, who has had major surveys at the Saint Louis Art Museum, the National Gallery of Art, and the di Rosa Center, works without preparatory sketches, letting each painting find its own logic as it's built up in the studio. The results — dense fields of interlocking shapes that read simultaneously as landscape, figure, and pure abstraction — reward the kind of slow looking that reveals new relationships the longer you stay with them.

This is Lisson's Hollywood outpost doing what it does well: giving a serious, underappreciated American painter room to be seen on his own terms, in a show that spans decades of a still-active and evolving practice.

shows.title: Thomas Demand
shows.description:
Thomas Demand doesn't photograph the world so much as he rebuilds it first. For decades the Berlin-based artist has recreated scenes from news media and everyday life as meticulous full-scale models made from paper and cardboard, then photographs the models and destroys them — leaving only the photograph as evidence of a scene that never quite existed in the first place.

This new body of work, spread across both of Matthew Marks' Los Angeles spaces, extends Demand's ongoing "Model Series" into new territory: fifteen photographs built from 18th- and 19th-century opera and ballet set models held in museum collections in Vienna, Monaco, and Munich, originally made for productions of Wagner's "Tannhäuser," Rossini's "Guillaume Tell," and period ballets. Using a periscope to navigate the tiny theatrical labyrinths, Demand lights and frames the miniature stage sets so they read as full-blown, dreamlike landscapes — a strange collapse of scale that turns nineteenth-century stagecraft into something genuinely eerie and cinematic. The show also includes newer photographs of Demand's own quotidian compositions — an overstuffed bookshelf, reeds on a pond — printed directly onto copper, a technique that nods back to Renaissance painting and early printmaking.

Demand's work has been the subject of one-person shows at MoMA, the Neue Nationalgalerie, and MOCA Tokyo, and a career retrospective is currently touring internationally. This Los Angeles exhibition overlaps with the show's related presentation at Vienna's MAK Museum, giving Angelenos a chance to see new photographic work from an artist still expanding what a "still life" or "history painting" can look like in the twenty-first century.

shows.title: MOCA's Collection at the Geffen
shows.description:
With the Confederate monuments of last season's blockbuster "Monuments" cleared out, MOCA turns its cavernous former police-car warehouse over to its own holdings. This is a collection show built for a big room: expect installation, scale, and media works from the 1960s onward rather than a tidy chronological survey, organized by Ann Goldstein and Bennett Simpson to show off the parts of MOCA's collection that don't fit neatly on the walls of the Grand Avenue building.

The Geffen has always been the site for MOCA's riskier, more physically ambitious programming, and a collection show here functions almost as a victory lap through four decades of acquisitions — the pieces that needed raw industrial space, high ceilings, and room to spread out. It's a chance to see both marquee names and newer additions to the collection in a setting Frank Gehry originally rigged up as a "temporary" contemporary space in 1983 and that somehow still feels like the most alive room in the museum's holdings.

Given the sheer square footage on offer, this is a show to wander rather than rush — one of those rare collection presentations that uses scale itself as a curatorial argument.

shows.title: Transmissions: Selections from the Marciano Collection
shows.description:
Housed in a former Scottish Rite Masonic temple on Wilshire Boulevard, the Marciano Art Foundation has assembled fifty-seven artists around a loose but generative idea: that art itself is a kind of transmission, a signal sent out into the world for someone else to receive. It's a broad enough premise to hold a lot of very different work, and the show uses that breadth well, moving from Mark Leckey's giant inflatable Felix the Cat — a nod to the character's use in NBC's first experimental television broadcasts in 1928 — to Thomas Struth's photographs of museum visitors looking at Velázquez, to Rosemarie Trockel's monumental machine-knitted wool paintings.

The strongest throughline is the show's interest in looking and being looked at. Deana Lawson's staged portrait of a mother and daughter, framed in mirrored glass, folds the viewer directly into the image; Barbara Kruger, Richard Prince, and Anne Collier all mine the vocabulary of advertising and pop culture to redirect its messages back at the audience. Elsewhere, artists use their own bodies as the signal: Kaari Upson's charcoal wall reliefs record the physical sweep of her arms, while Glenn Ligon's coal-dust text paintings channel James Baldwin's writing on race and belonging directly onto the wall.

Curated by Hanneke Skerath and Douglas Fogle, Transmissions draws entirely from the deep holdings of the Marciano family's private collection, and the resulting checklist reads like a who's-who of the last three decades of blue-chip contemporary practice — Levine, Tillmans, Demand, Otto-Knapp, Walther — installed inside one of the city's strangest and most theatrical exhibition buildings. It's a long-running installation, on view for well over two years, which makes it an easy one to build a visit around.

shows.title: Autumn Enchantment
shows.description:
bG Gallery has always leaned into the open-call, international-roster model, and Autumn Enchantment is that approach in its purest form: a themed group exhibition, curated by Om Bleicher, Yelena Lev, and Lark Pilinsky, that invited artists from anywhere in the world to respond to the idea of autumn as metaphor. Presented in collaboration with Vivid Art Studio Gallery and Lark Gallery, the show pairs a physical installation at Bergamot Station with a parallel online presentation, so the roster skews wider and more varied than a typical single-gallery show.

The connecting thread is loose by design — transition, memory, renewal, the sense of something ending in order to become something else — which gives participating artists room to interpret the season through very different media and visual languages rather than converging on a single house style. It's less about a unified argument than a mood: a gathering of works meant to be looked at slowly, with the kind of unhurried attention the season itself is supposed to invite.

As one of the anchor spaces at Bergamot Station, one of the Westside's longest-running gallery complexes, bG Gallery has built a reputation on exactly this kind of accessible, community-oriented programming — shows that prioritize breadth of participation over market pedigree.
